It's really useful, though tricky to learn. I advise watching youtube tutorials over just reading the online manual, because the terminology used isn't suitable for true beginners to 3D modelling.

I have used Blender numerous times to make models for the Sims 4 mods, Skyrim Mods, and just fun experimentation.

With the program being open source, there's a huge amount of plug-ins and add-ons that you can get for it, both free or paid. If you're into 3D printing, there's a plug-in that'll help you convert to STL. Curious about rigging/animation? There's plug-ins that help streamline both processes.

Other 3D model/animation programs on the market are ludicrously priced, over-complicated, or vastly limited by being closed-source. Honestly, I don't know what I would be doing without Blender; I use it every day for my work, and for fun.

So, it doesn't matter what part of the 3D model/animation world you're dappling in, Blender is a fantastic program to start out with.

It is easily the most powerful, feature-packed piece of software on the planet that is completely free, open-source, and maintained by absolute legends. Modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, node-based shaders, VFX, video editing, geometry nodes—it does literally everything. If Adobe or Autodesk owned this software, they would charge you $80 a month and your left kidney.

The catch? The UI learning curve isn't a hill—it's a vertical cliff made of hot glass.

Your first five hours consist of opening the program, staring at a grey default cube, accidentally hitting X to delete it, pressing a random hotkey, inverting your normal vectors into the 4th dimension, watching your entire UI split into forty tiny useless windows, and closing the program in a cold sweat.

Every single person who uses Blender goes through the exact same rite of passage: watching Andrew Price (Blender Guru) build a glazed donut on YouTube for eight hours straight just to figure out how to extrude a face.

Downsized my cube, accidentally joined two meshes together with non-manifold geometry, spent 3 hours node-wrangling a procedural wood texture, set my render samples to 4096, melted my graphics card, and created a lumpy pink donut.

10/10. Will delete the default cube again tomorrow.

As a 3D artist with 3 years of experience, I can confidently say Blender is one of the most powerful tools I’ve ever worked with. It’s open-source and completely free, yet capable of professional-grade results in modeling, sculpting, animation, rendering, and more. With the right settings, the render quality is absolutely stunning, and the ecosystem of add-ons (both free and paid) takes it even further.

What really sets Blender apart is its accessibility beginners can pick it up quickly, and advanced users can push it to production-level standards. Every skill I’ve needed to learn has been available through free YouTube tutorials, making it an invaluable resource for both learning and creating. For me, it’s been an essential part of my workflow from personal experiments to client projects. So those who wanna try out 3d, sure go ahead and try this software.

Blender is a great tool for different purposes, whether it be for personal or public use, making 3d/2d art/animation, or making models and goofing around. You'll also need a decent computer since Blender may take a lot processing power.

This software is a legendary creation and a gift to all those who use it.
When you open it initially and spend your first ten hours in it, you'll often feel out of your element, but with time you will learn how important this is to the freelance artist.
Blender has modeling capabilities, everyone is aware of this. Other features that often get overlooked is the sculpting, UV unwrapping capabilities, texturing with nodes (this is tough but there's a surplus of tutorials out there), rigging, animation, storyboarding, video editing, etc.
This program is really something you should at least explore, as it competes with the industry standard software(Maya,ZBrush to name a few) while being provided at no cost. 

TLDR: Good program, hard to understand at first, see tutorials.

I love Steam (albeit with a lot of pain) and I love Blender. I've been using Blender on Steam for quite a long time.

CON: Steam will update your copy of Blender with no clear method of restoring an old version.

When it updated from v2.80 to v2.81, the way EEVEE renders (shadows in particular) changed in a way that practically invalidated my animation that I was partway through rendering and compositing over the course of many sessions.

I had to find a legitimate older copy of Blender v2.80 to finish the animation I was working on. The difficulty in doing so is not relevant to here.

Blender is great. Blender is powerful. Blender gets better every update.

Just don't use Steam to run Blender. I'll continue doing so, but only out of habit. I might transition eventually, but heed my warning: If you continue and install/use Blender in Steam it can be somewhat hazardous to any projects you are working on.
